title: Joshua 5:1–9
context: Joshua 5:1–9 follows the crossing of the Jordan. The kings of the Amorites and Canaanites lose heart when they hear what the LORD has done, and at that moment the LORD commands Israel to circumcise the generation born in the wilderness. The narrator explains why it is needed: the men who left Egypt died because they did not listen to the LORD, and their sons were never circumcised on the way. The LORD then declares the reproach of Egypt rolled away, which gives Gilgal its name. Both traditions read the passage as covenant renewal before conquest, with Israel’s identity as the LORD’s people restored before any battle is fought.

verses.text: When all the kings of the Amorites, who were beyond the Jordan westward, and all the kings of the Canaanites, who were by the sea, heard how the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan from before the children of Israel until we had crossed over, their heart melted, and there was no more spirit in them, because of the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: The Amorite and Canaanite kings lose heart because they hear what the LORD did at the Jordan. Arminian readers note that God’s acts are made known to the nations, as Rahab already confessed (Joshua 2:9–11), so even Israel’s enemies hear the evidence and are left accountable for their response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that the melting of hearts is the LORD’s work going ahead of Israel, as promised (Deuteronomy 2:25; 11:25). The WEB reads "until we had crossed over," following one Hebrew reading. Both traditions see that the victory is God’s before the first battle.

verses.text: At that time, the LORD said to Joshua, “Make flint knives, and circumcise again the sons of Israel the second time.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD commands Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise Israel "the second time," meaning a renewed mass circumcision rather than circumcising anyone twice. Arminians see God renewing his covenant with a new generation that must now take up its sign before entering the conflict.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the timing as significant: in sight of the enemy, Israel is made vulnerable rather than battle-ready, because its first need is covenant faithfulness. Both traditions read the sign as God’s claim on his people, pointing to circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 10:16; 30:6).

verses.text: Joshua made himself flint knives, and circumcised the sons of Israel at the hill of the foreskins.
verses.arminianNotes: Joshua obeys immediately and circumcises the men at a place named for the act, the hill of the foreskins. Arminian readers see Joshua’s prompt obedience as a model of a leader who acts on God’s word without delay, even when the timing seems militarily unwise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the covenant sign is applied to the whole people at God’s command and through his appointed leader. Both traditions see the episode as a corporate act that marks the whole nation, not only individuals, as belonging to the LORD.

verses.text: This is the reason Joshua circumcised them: all the people who came out of Egypt, who were males, even all the men of war, died in the wilderness along the way, after they came out of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The narrator explains the reason: the men who came out of Egypt, including all the men of war, died in the wilderness. Arminians read this as a reminder that the exodus generation forfeited the land through unbelief (Numbers 14:28–35), a warning that privilege does not replace faithful response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree on the judgment and also stress that God’s purpose did not fail with that generation, since he raised up their children to inherit the promise. Both traditions read the verse in light of Hebrews 3:16–19, which applies the wilderness deaths as a warning against unbelief.

verses.text: For all the people who came out were circumcised; but all the people who were born in the wilderness along the way as they came out of Egypt had not been circumcised.
verses.arminianNotes: Those who left Egypt had been circumcised, but the children born in the wilderness had not. Arminian readers note that the text records the lapse without explaining its cause, and they draw the general lesson that covenant signs can be neglected while a generation is under discipline.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that the text gives no reason for the lapse and avoid speculating about it. Some connect it with the wilderness judgment as a time when covenant life was suspended. Both traditions see God restoring what was neglected as the people cross into the promised land.

verses.text: For the children of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness until all the nation, even the men of war who came out of Egypt, were consumed, because they didn’t listen to the LORD’s voice. The LORD swore to them that he wouldn’t let them see the land which the LORD swore to their fathers that he would give us, a land flowing with milk and honey.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel wandered forty years until the men of war were consumed because they didn’t listen to the LORD’s voice, and the LORD swore they would not see the land. Arminians read this as God’s just response to persistent disobedience, showing that his promise to the nation did not guarantee every individual a share in it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the judgment was just and add that the same verse affirms the oath to the fathers, which God keeps by giving the land to the next generation. Both traditions hold the warning and the faithfulness of God together, and both note the phrase "a land flowing with milk and honey."

verses.text: Their children, whom he raised up in their place, were circumcised by Joshua, for they were uncircumcised, because they had not circumcised them on the way.
verses.arminianNotes: The children whom God raised up in their place are now circumcised by Joshua. Arminians emphasize that each generation must embrace the covenant for itself, and here a new generation takes on the sign their parents had failed to give them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress the phrase "whom he raised up in their place": God himself provides the heirs of his promise. Both traditions see covenant continuity across generations as God’s gift, received by the people in obedience to his command.

verses.text: When they were done circumcising the whole nation, they stayed in their places in the camp until they were healed.
verses.arminianNotes: The whole nation stays in the camp until it heals, defenseless within reach of Jericho. Arminian readers see trust on display: the people put their safety in God’s hands rather than in their own readiness for battle, as the covenant required of them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and point to God’s protection over a vulnerable people, since the enemy’s hearts had already melted (5:1). Both traditions read the healing period as a lesson that God’s people are secured by his care before they are ever called to act.

verses.text: The LORD said to Joshua, “Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you.” Therefore the name of that place was called Gilgal to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has rolled away the reproach of Egypt, and the place is named Gilgal, which sounds like the Hebrew for "roll." Arminians read the reproach as the shame of slavery and of the wilderness years, now lifted as Israel stands in the land as God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree. Some read the reproach as Egypt’s taunt that Israel’s God could not bring them in (compare Exodus 32:12; Numbers 14:13–16), and others as the shame of the slave years. Both traditions see God himself removing Israel’s disgrace and the name of the place preserving the memory.
